newsitem.title: UK: Cassell sells children's book unit to Penguin.
newsitem.headline: Cassell sells children's book unit to Penguin.

text.p: British publisher Cassell Plc said on Tuesday it had agreed to sell its Victor Gollancz children's list to the Penguin group for 870,000 stg.
Cassell said the list had a turnover of just 885,000 stg last year, leaving it with the option of expanding it significantly or selling it.
Cassell has decided to sell in order to focus on academic and adult general publishing. The sale to Pearson's Penguin unit is conditional on a number of consents.
Cassell reported a return to operating profit in 1996, moving from a loss of 43,000 stg in 1995 to a profit of 1.15 million last year.
It maintained its dividend at 3.0 pence per share for a total of 4.5p. Cassell shares added 6.5p to 91.5p on the back of the results.
The publisher, whose authors include Britain's Nick Hornby, said that sales and margins in early 1997 had been ahead of last year.

The release of the film version of Fever Pitch, Hornby's autobiographical tale of the life of a football fan, has helped to return the title to the non-fiction paperback top 10. It has also stimulated sales of Hornby's High Fidelity novel.
Cassell chairman and chief executive Philip Sturrock said the company had benefited from the scrapping in 1995 of the Net Book Agreement, a price-fixing pact among publishers.
"Our sales to the big chains have gone up and we've managed to get good displays for our new paperback imprints, Indigo and Vista".
Sturrock said that Cassell wanted eventually to build its academic and religious titles to a point where they were supplying around 50 percent of turnover, rather than the current 20 percent.
He said Cassell would seek acquisitions to help move towards this goal, noting the higher margins and better backlist sales on such titles.
